title: The Definite Article
subtitle: ὁ, ἡ, τό — the gateway to declension.
objectives: Decline the definite article in all three genders, both numbers, all five cases.
Recognize the article as the most common word in Greek prose.
Understand that Greek has no indefinite article (no word for 'a' or 'an').
Observe the pattern that will recur in the first and second declension nouns.

sections.heading: The article
sections.body:
Greek has a definite article: ὁ, ἡ, τό (the). It has no indefinite article. When you want to say 'a man' in Greek, you just say ἄνθρωπος with no article. When you want to say 'the man', you say ὁ ἄνθρωπος.

The article agrees with its noun in gender, number, and case. That means the article changes its ending to match the noun. If the noun is masculine singular nominative, the article is ὁ. If the noun is feminine plural genitive, the article is τῶν. The article has twenty-four forms: three genders, two numbers, five cases.

The article is the most common word in Greek prose. In any paragraph of Plato or Xenophon, you will see it dozens of times. Learn it now, and you have the skeleton for the first and second declension nouns.

sections.heading: The twenty-four forms
sections.body:
Masculine:
              singular    plural
  nominative  ὁ           οἱ
  genitive    τοῦ         τῶν
  dative      τῷ          τοῖς
  accusative  τόν         τούς
  vocative    (none)      (none)

Feminine:
              singular    plural
  nominative  ἡ           αἱ
  genitive    τῆς         τῶν
  dative      τῇ          ταῖς
  accusative  τήν         τάς
  vocative    (none)      (none)

Neuter:
              singular    plural
  nominative  τό          τά
  genitive    τοῦ         τῶν
  dative      τῷ          τοῖς
  accusative  τό          τά
  vocative    (none)      (none)

The article has no vocative. You do not use the article when addressing someone directly.

Notice the pattern: the genitive plural is τῶν for all three genders. The dative plural masculine and neuter is τοῖς. The endings will recur when you learn the nouns.

sections.heading: An example from Xenophon
sections.body: Anabasis I.1.1 begins: Δαρείου καὶ Παρυσάτιδος γίγνονται παῖδες δύο. The word order is flexible, but if we render it in the most common order: 'Of Darius and Parysatis are born two sons.' No article on παῖδες because it is indefinite. If Xenophon had written οἱ παῖδες, it would mean 'the sons' — specific, known sons. Greek uses the presence or absence of the article to mark definiteness.

sections.heading: Self-check
sections.instructions: Cover the answers. Write out the requested forms from memory.

items.prompt: Does Greek have an indefinite article?
items.answer: No. To say 'a man', you just say ἄνθρωπος with no article.

items.prompt: Does the article have a vocative form?
Which form of the article is the same for masculine and neuter in the genitive singular?
Which form of the article is the same for all three genders in the genitive plural?
What does the article agree with?
items.answer: The noun — in gender, number, and case.

sections.heading: Up next
sections.body: Lesson 2.2 introduces the second declension masculine nouns: ὁ ἄνθρωπος, ὁ λόγος, ὁ ἵππος. These nouns follow the same pattern as the masculine article. Once you have the article and the second declension, you will be able to read simple noun phrases and to understand the function of the nominative and accusative cases.

lesson_completion.criteria: Mark the lesson complete when you can write out all twenty-four forms of the article from memory in under five minutes with no more than two errors.
